where: Section 2, sentence after the neutral-axis formula ("When I_xy ≠ 0, this line is not perpendicular to the moment vector")
problem: Wrong geometric statement, and it contradicts the lead of the chapter. In symmetric bending about a principal axis the neutral axis lies along the moment vector (M_x only, I_xy = 0 gives α = 0, i.e. the neutral axis is the x-axis, the same line as the moment vector). So the neutral axis is never perpendicular to the moment vector; what is true is that it is no longer perpendicular to the plane of the applied moment (it no longer lies along the moment vector). A student will memorise "perpendicular becomes non-perpendicular" and get the geometry backwards.
fix: When I_xy ≠ 0 the neutral axis is no longer perpendicular to the plane of the applied moment: it tilts away from the direction of the moment vector, which is the line it follows in symmetric bending. With only M_x, tan α = I_xy / I_yy: the tilt comes directly from the product second moment.

problem: Both the question ("why is the neutral axis not perpendicular to the moment vector") and the answer ("the two directions coincide only when I_xy = 0") are false. With I_xy = 0 and both M_x and M_y acting, tan α = −(M_y I_xx)/(M_x I_yy) while the moment vector has tan β = M_y/M_x, so the two directions do not coincide unless the moment acts about one principal axis only. Conversely, for special combinations of M_x and M_y they do coincide even when I_xy ≠ 0. The stated rule is wrong in both directions.
fix: Q6: Why does the neutral axis tilt away from the moment vector when I_xy ≠ 0? Answer: the neutral-axis direction is tan α = −k₁/k₂, and both k₁ and k₂ contain I_xy, so the line rotates when I_xy changes; the moment-vector direction tan β = M_y/M_x does not depend on the section. The two directions coincide only in the special case of a moment about a single principal axis (M_y = 0 with I_xy = 0, giving α = β = 0).

problem: The sign statement is reversed under the chapter's own formula tan 2θ_p = −2I_xy/(I_xx − I_yy). With I_xx = I_yy and I_xy > 0, 2θ_p → −90°, so θ_p = −45°, and it is this −45° that gives I_u = I + I_xy = I_max. Saying "the sign follows the sign of I_xy" pairs I_max with the wrong angle.
fix: C = I, R = |I_xy|, I_max = I + |I_xy|, I_min = I − |I_xy|. tan 2θ_p is infinite, so |θ_p| = 45°; with this chapter's formula the sign of θ_p is opposite to the sign of I_xy (I_xy > 0 gives θ_p = −45°, which is the direction of I_max). Substitute θ_p back to confirm I_uv = 0.

problem: The two moment-resolution formulas and the two-term stress formula depend on which way the axes are rotated, but the coordinate rotation is never written down. A reader cannot tell whether u = x cos θ_p + y sin θ_p or the mirror version, and so cannot reproduce the signs of M_u, M_v and of the stress terms.
fix: State the rotation once, before the formulas: u = x cos θ_p + y sin θ_p, v = −x sin θ_p + y cos θ_p, so the u-axis is at θ_p from the x-axis. With this rotation M_u = ∫σ v dA = M_x cos θ_p − M_y sin θ_p and M_v = ∫σ u dA = M_x sin θ_p + M_y cos θ_p, which is why σ = (M_u/I_u)v + (M_v/I_v)u.

problem: Quantities in the figure notes carry no units and use computer notation, while the text uses m⁴ and powers of ten.

where: Section 2, sentence "Some syllabi call this the k method; others call it the neutral axis method"
problem: Neither name is a recognised textbook name for this formula; the claim about syllabi is unsupported and may confuse a student looking the topic up elsewhere.
fix: Drop the naming claim. Say simply: this is the general centroidal (product-of-inertia) formula; with I_xy = 0 it reduces to σ = M_x y/I_xx + M_y x/I_yy about principal axes.
